combined_analysis:
**Root cause of rollout_1 failure (83.3%):** The agent attempted to approve ALL 26 pending Venmo payment requests before establishing which ones came from roommates/coworkers. This 'act first, filter later' approach caused irreversible state changes — 15 of the 26 pending requests disappeared between the first fetch and the second fetch (likely approved or state-corrupted by the initial bulk approval attempt). When the agent finally implemented proper filtering, only 4 of the expected 10 matching requests remained pending. It approved those 4 correctly, but the total approved set did not match the expected 10 IDs (the failed test: 'assert set of updated payment request ids match exactly').

**Success factor in rollout_2 (100%):** The agent followed a correct sequence: (1) gathered roommate/coworker emails from phone contacts, (2) fetched all 26 pending payment requests, (3) filtered to 10 matching requests, (4) approved only those 10. Since filtering happened BEFORE any approval actions, the state was clean and exactly the right set was approved.

**The critical ordering pattern:** For bulk actions with eligibility criteria, the agent must ALWAYS resolve eligibility criteria and filter BEFORE taking any actions. Actions are often irreversible (approving a payment request cannot be undone). If the agent acts on all items first and filters afterward, it risks (a) modifying ineligible items, (b) corrupting state so eligible items become unfindable, and (c) producing a modified set that doesn't match expectations.

**Missing playbook guidance:** There is no entry covering the 'filter before act' principle for bulk operations. Entry [9f8d858f] addresses criteria extraction from conversation context, but its trigger ('responding to a contact's request') is too narrow. The needed rule applies whenever a task requires performing the same action on a SUBSET of items matching specific criteria — the agent must build the filtered list as an intermediate artifact BEFORE executing any actions.

**PP trace corroboration:** The supplementary trace shows the same anti-pattern — the agent approved all 26 requests without filtering (17 succeeded before balance ran out), then tried to top up and approve the rest. It happened to approve the right ones among others, but would likely fail the exact-match test. This confirms the failure mode is systematic, not a fluke.

**Additional observation:** Rollout_1 also suffered from a token copy-paste error (step 12 had a corrupted token string), wasting steps. Using stored variables rather than manual copy-paste (per entry [c3efc092]) would have avoided this, but it didn't contribute to the core failure.

---

Both rollouts followed the same correct high-level strategy: (1) find Leslie Ball in phone contacts, (2) read text messages to discover she asked for Peter Jackson movie recommendations, (3) search SimpleNote for the 'Movie Recommendations' note, (4) parse note content to extract Peter Jackson-directed movies, (5) send comma-separated titles to Leslie, (6) call complete_task(). Both extracted the same 3 movies and sent the same message to the same phone number (text_message_id 16803 in both cases).

The 12.5% gap (7/8 vs 8/8) came from a single test: `assert model changes match phone.GlobalTextMessage, phone.UserTextMessage`. All content and structural tests passed in both rollouts — the correct movies were sent to the correct person. The failing test validates that the COMPLETE SET of model record changes matches expectations, not just the content.

Root cause analysis: Despite exhaustive comparison, both rollouts made the same meaningful state-changing API calls (3 phone logins, 3 simple_note logins, 1 send_text_message, 1 complete_task). The only structural difference is that rollout 1 performed an additional paginated contact search (2 pages) in the same code block where it sent the message, while rollout 2 hardcoded the already-known phone number. However, search_contacts is a GET request that should not modify model state. The failure likely reflects either environmental non-determinism or a very subtle ordering/timing effect invisible from the traces.

Playbook effectiveness: The existing entries were well-applied. The problem-solving workflow [9f8d858f] correctly guided the agent to read messages first. Pagination [6c139a99] was correctly used. Credentials were fetched from supervisor [867f30db]. The complete_task entry [78832af2] was correctly applied (no answer argument for an action-only task).

The PP trace annotations confirm the agent followed the playbook ('Following entry [Problem Solving Heuristics And Workflows]: gather data then apply criteria') and was uncertain only about message formatting ('Need to confirm phone send_text_message expects access_token and message fields'), which was resolved correctly by reading API docs.

No clear generalizable rule is missing. Both rollouts demonstrated correct application of existing guidance. The single test failure does not indicate a systematic gap — it appears environmental rather than strategic.

proposed.content: When a task requires performing an action (approve, delete, update, send) on a SUBSET of items matching criteria: (1) Resolve ALL filter criteria first (e.g., fetch contact lists, relationship categories, tags). (2) Fetch the COMPLETE set of candidate items. (3) Apply filters and build an explicit filtered list — print it as a verification artifact before proceeding. (4) Execute actions ONLY on items in the filtered list. NEVER act on all items first and filter afterward — many actions (approvals, deletions, payments) are irreversible and premature bulk actions can corrupt state so eligible items become unfindable on re-fetch.
proposed.rationale: Rollout_1 of the Venmo task approved all 26 pending requests before filtering to roommates/coworkers, causing irreversible state corruption; only 4 of 10 expected requests remained when filtering was finally applied. Rollout_2 filtered first and approved exactly the right 10. Entry [9f8d858f] covers criteria extraction from conversation context but is too narrowly scoped to cover this general bulk-action ordering invariant.
